profile.summary: Romans is a theological letter in which Paul exposes the gospel of Christ as God's decisive revelation to the world. He starts from the human situation under sin, shows that no one is justified by works of the law and presents salvation as a gift received by faith in Jesus Christ. The letter also deals with the security of salvation, God's faithfulness to his promises to Israel, the life transformed by the gospel and unity between Jewish and Gentile believers in the church of Rome. The introduction of the source suggests a probable date around 57 AD, written during Paul's stay in Corinth, although some historical details are inferred and not absolutely certain.
profile.setting: The letter is born in a context of tension in the church of Rome. The community had probably grown from converts linked to Pentecost and organized into several domestic churches. After the expulsion of the Jews from Rome by Claudius in 49 AD, the Gentile Christians gained prominence; when the Jews returned, a division between the Gentile majority and the Judeo-Christian minority arose, especially as to the permanence of the law of Moses in Christian life. Paul, who still did not know Rome personally, probably writes of Corinth, near the end of his third missionary journey, with plans to go to Jerusalem, then to Rome and finally to Spain. As for authorship and date, the letter is attributed to Paul, and the most likely date is about 57 AD, but this is reconstructed from internal indications.

structure.label: Greeting and theme
structure.description: Paul presents himself, greets the recipients, thanks for their faith and announces the central theme: the gospel of Christ.

structure.label: The Universal Need for the Gospel
structure.description: Human guilt before God is exposed, encompassing Gentiles and Jews, until the conclusion that all are under sin and no one is justified by works.

structure.label: Justification by faith and Abraham
structure.description: Paul shows that the righteousness of God comes by faith, without room for boasting, and uses Abraham to highlight the principle of faith.

structure.label: Security of the salvation
structure.description: The letter develops the fruits of justification: peace with God, a contrast between Adam and Christ, the inability of sin and the law to thwart the divine purpose, and the liberating action of the Spirit that sustains the future hope.

structure.label: God's fidelity to Israel
structure.description: Paul argues that God has not failed in his promises: there is a remnant, the unbelief of many Jews is responsible for the very rejection of Christ, and God still has purposes for Israel.

structure.label: Life and unity in the church
structure.description: The gospel produces a new way of thinking and living, marked by service, love, submission to the authorities and harmonious coexistence; then Paul applies this to the conflict between believers about practices linked to the law, calling them to the mutual welcome and example of Christ.

structure.label: Conclusion
structure.description: Paul closes with references to his ministry, greetings to co-workers, final warning and doxology.

themes: Universality of sin and necessity of grace
Fidelity of God to Bible Promises
Unity between Jews and Gentiles in the Church
readingKeys: Notice how Paul alternates between doctrinal exposition and practical application, without separating theology and Christian life.
Pay attention to the contrast between Jews and Gentiles: the letter responds to a concrete division of the church of Rome.
Read chapters 12 to 15 as a necessary consequence of the gospel, and not as a disconnected moral appendix.
profile.cautions: The introduction of the source presents debates of interpretation: the classical reading of the Reformation emphasizes the individual justification by faith, while more recent readings also highlight the question of the inclusion of the Gentiles and the continuity of the people of God. The best reading, according to the source itself, combines these perspectives. Some historical data - such as the exact origin of Christianity in Rome and the precise date of the letter is likely, but not absolutely certain.

dossier.narratedEra: Imperial Rome in the time of Claudius and then, in the period when Christianity already exists as a movement in homes of the capital. The background narrated in the notes is the 1st century AD, with emphasis on the expulsion of the Jews from Rome in A.D. 49 and the later return of many of them before the writing of the letter.
dossier.compositionEra: Probably about A.D. 57, when Paul was in Corinth, at the end of his third missionary journey and before moving to Jerusalem; the notes also place the text at a time when Paul had already acted widely in the Eastern Mediterranean and planned to visit Rome and then Spain.

politics.title: Decree of Claudius and impact on the Roman community
politics.detail: The notes claim that Emperor Claudius expelled all Jews from Rome in A.D. 49, including Christian Jews; then the decree expired and many returned.
politics.readingImpact: This helps explain why the church of Rome was marked by leadership changes and a tense internal composition between Jewish and Gentile Christians.

politics.title: Temporary Gentile dominance in the church of Rome
politics.detail: When Paul writes, the Gentile Christians had taken over the leadership of the community during the absence of many Jews expelled.
politics.readingImpact: The dispute over continuity with the Law of Moses gains social contour: the theme is not only doctrinal, but also of authority within the church.

politics.title: Roman Empire as a framework for mission and mobility
politics.detail: The notes place the writing in the world of the Roman Empire, with references to provinces, port cities and networks of displacement (Corinto, Cêncrea, Jerusalem, Illyricum, Rome, Spain).
politics.readingImpact: The imperial map gives meaning to Paul's missionary strategy and the fact that the letter aimed at a church in the imperial capital.

politics.title: Citizenship and Greco-Roman culture of adoption
politics.detail: Commenting on the adoption in Rom 8:15, the note relies on the Greco-Roman custom, noting that even the imperial family practiced adoption; mentions Julius Caesar adopting Otavian, then Augustus.
politics.readingImpact: The metaphor of adoption communicates not only affection, but legal status and privileges of heir, illuminating the language of affiliation in Romans.

politics.title: Magistrature and civic elite in Corinth
politics.detail: The mention of Erastus is linked to a possible Corinthian inscription and a post of magistrate of the city, although the identification is cautious.
politics.readingImpact: It suggests that Paul's network of collaborators crossed different social and administrative levels of the Roman urban world.

customs.title: Domestic Churches in Rome
customs.detail: The notes say that Christians did not have large buildings for worship; they gathered in private houses, and Rome had several "house churches."
customs.readingImpact: The reading of Romans 14-16 gains a concrete community aspect: the appeal to unity is addressed to small but connected groups, which met in different homes.

customs.title: Sponsorship and material aid
customs.detail: Phoebe is described as a patron, someone of possessions and influence who helped people and causes with his own resources.
customs.readingImpact: This clarifies why Paul recommends it prominently and shows how the ministry depended on networks of material and social support.

customs.title: Meals, hospitality and home relations
customs.detail: Gaius is called Paul's host, and the very salutation structure in Romans 16 shows domestic hospitality as a visible Christian practice.
customs.readingImpact: The letter does not circulate in a vacuum; it presupposes visits, lodging and personal ties as part of ecclesial life.

customs.title: Greeting with holy kiss
customs.detail: The "Bbeijo" is presented as a common form of greeting in the ancient world, especially among Jews, and then Christian liturgical pattern.
customs.readingImpact: The final commandment in Rom 16:16 shows how everyday practices of honor and peace were Christianized to express fellowship.

customs.title: Culture of ministerial and scribe work
customs.detail: Tércio is identified as the Amanuense who wrote the letter under Paul's saying; the notes note that this type of scribe was common in the old letters.
customs.readingImpact: Helps to read Romans as a carefully composed document, mediated by an ancient epistolary process, not as an informal improvisation.

customs.title: Life of Jewish diaspora and migratory returns
customs.detail: Priscilla and Aquila are remembered as a couple who left Rome, worked with Paul in Corinth and Ephesus and then returned to Rome.
customs.readingImpact: The mobility of people explains how Paul knew so many Roman Christians without visiting the city before.

language.title: Epistolar structure and chart frame
language.detail: The notes highlight the normal pattern of introduction of New Testament letters: sender, recipients, thanksgiving and theme; they also note that the final doxology resumes themes from the beginning.
language.readingImpact: This helps to read Romans as a carefully architected argument, with beginning and end talking to each other.

language.title: "Slave of Christ Jesus" as a language of total service
language.detail: The term "slave" is linked to Old Testament leaders called God's servants, emphasizing complete submission to Christ.
language.readingImpact: Paul's self-presentation is not only honorific; it defines apostolic authority as obedient service.

language.title: "Fail and obedience" as a framework of the mission
language.detail: The notes say that Paul wants to lead the Gentiles to believe and obey, and that this creates a frame of the book between Rom 1:5 and 16:26.
language.readingImpact: The letter should be read as called the faith expressed in obedience, not as mere religious theory.

language.title: "Righteousness of God" and forensic language
language.detail: The expression is explained how he puts us in the right position before God, originating in the court and root in the Old Testament.
language.readingImpact: This directs 1:17 reading to the theme of justification and not for generic moral improvement.

language.title: "Flesh" and earthly life
language.detail: "Flesh" is explained as a bodily existence in this world in Rom 1:3; in Rm 8, "Physamino" nature expresses human slavery to sin.
language.readingImpact: The language of the letter distinguishes common human existence from sinful dominion, which affects the reading of incarnation, sin and life in the Spirit.

language.title: Vice List and Hellenistic Literary Resource
language.detail: The list of sins in Rom 1:29-31 is described as a popular literary form of the Hellenistic, non-exhaustive world.
language.readingImpact: This shows that Paul uses a recognizable moral catalogue to intensify the universal accusation against humanity.

timeline.title: AD 49: Expulsion of Jews from Rome by Claudius
timeline.detail: The notes place the expulsion as a key event for the later composition of Romans, affecting even Jewish Christians such as Priscilla and Aquila.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone helps to understand the recomposition of the Roman church and the tension between Jews and Gentiles when Paul writes.

timeline.title: After A.D. 49: gradual return of Christian Jews
timeline.detail: Claudius' decree would have fallen into disuse, allowing the return of many Christian Jews to Rome before the letter.
timeline.readingImpact: The return of the Jews explains why a Judeo-Christian minority could return to the place of the Law in the community.

timeline.title: About AD 57: writing in Corinth
timeline.detail: The introduction of Tyndale and Matthew Henry place the letter around AD 57 or 56, during a stay in Corinth at the end of the third missionary journey.
timeline.readingImpact: The date fits Romans at the time when Paul concludes his work in the east and prepares new missionary fronts.

timeline.title: Next trip to Jerusalem to deliver an offer
timeline.detail: Paul planned to bring to Jerusalem a collection of Gentile churches for the poor believers there.
timeline.readingImpact: The letter is born at the intersection between mission, interecclesial communion and financial accountability.

timeline.title: Later project: visit to Rome and mission to Spain
timeline.detail: The notes say that Rome was an intermediate parade, and Paul's final goal was Spain, where Christ had not yet been announced.
timeline.readingImpact: Romans also works as a letter of presentation and missionary support for a front not yet evangelized.

timeline.title: End of the third missionary journey as an immediate horizon
timeline.detail: The geographical references of Rom 15:19-24 are presented as a setback on Paul's ministry from Jerusalem to Illyricum and as a bridge to new steps.
timeline.readingImpact: This makes Romans apostolic balance sheet text: completed missionary past and open missionary future.

investigation: The exact chronology depends on indirect historical reconstruction; the notes speak in "Around AD 57" and "AD 56" without trying to fix a day or month.
The traditional authorship paulina is assumed throughout the introduction consulted; there is no substantive alternative debate on authorship or pseudepigraphy in the notes.
The hypothesis that chapter 16 would belong to another letter is mentioned only as speculation without solid manuscript support.
The identification of Erastus with the Corinthian officer is presented with caution; the note itself uses probabilistic language.

Confessional reading is recognized in the notes: Romans is read both in the key of the Reformation and by contemporary approaches focused on Jews and Gentiles, and the two are considered partially true.
The notes deal with social and ecclesial issues based on selected details; they do not provide a complete panorama of Roman life, the Judaism of the diaspora or the imperial administration.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends strictly on the attached notes and therefore covers only what they really mention. There are gaps on broader Roman politics, detailed economic practices, and the social context of Rome beyond what is necessary for Romans. In language and customs, only terms and customs explicitly commented on the notes were included; no etymologies, alternative translations or additional historical reconstructions were inferred. In timeline, we prefer approximate dates and formulations discussed when the notes themselves were cautious. There was also no intersection with other external sources, and events from other Bible books were used only when the notes quoted them directly to explain Romans.
